paragraphs.text: The page puts four pictures in front of you and asks the same question four times: a patient with a doctor's appointment at 10:45, colleagues waiting in a bar at 20:00, a meeting in an office at 9:00, and two friends cooking for a third who is expected at 20:00. Mark on the timeline how many minutes each person may be late, then compare with a partner. You will disagree, and the disagreement is the point.

In German, as anywhere, lateness is read as a signal rather than a number. Ten minutes at the surgery can mean the slot goes to somebody else, because {{de:Der Arzt hat um 10:45 Uhr einen Termin}} and the next patient is already in the waiting room. Ten minutes in a bar is a non-event. A meeting in der Firma sits somewhere in between, and arriving at a friend's dinner table with flowers in your hand and an apology on your lips is survivable exactly once.
Herr Spiegel hat um 10:45 Uhr einen Termin beim Arzt. Pia ist noch nicht da — der Termin war um 20:00 Uhr. Frau Moser kommt zu spät zur Besprechung. Leo kommt zum Essen, Lena und Stefan warten.

So before you learn the apology, learn the scale. The box on the page gives you the two conversions German uses when it counts lateness out loud: 60 seconds make a minute, and 30 minutes make {{de:eine halbe Stunde}}. Saying {{de:Ich bin eine halbe Stunde zu spät}} is a much bigger admission than {{de:Ich bin zehn Minuten zu spät}}, and both are things you will actually have to say.

items.german: Es tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.
items.english: I am sorry, I am late.
Next time please be on time!

blocks.passage: Frau Moser kommt zehn Minuten zu spät zur Besprechung in der Firma.
blocks.prompt: What does Frau Moser say when she walks in?
options: Es tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.
blocks.explanationEnglish: The late person is the one who apologizes. The other two lines are replies — one from the person who was kept waiting, one accepting an apology.

concept.title: entschuldigen und antworten
concept.rule: The person who is late opens with an apology; the person who waited answers. German uses a soft third-person impersonal form — Es tut mir leid, literally it does me sorrow — rather than a direct I am sorry, and the answer is short: Kein Problem, Schon gut or Macht nichts.
concept.exampleGerman: Es tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät. — Macht nichts.
concept.exampleEnglish: I am sorry, I am late. — It doesn't matter.

blocks.prompt: Match the German phrase to its meaning.

paragraphs.text: Fifteen seconds per pair is the right rhythm here. These eight phrases are what a waiting person and a late person say to each other, so they are worth knowing as a set rather than one by one.

pairs.german: Es tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.
pairs.english: I am sorry, I am late.
Next time please be on time!

pairs.german: Ich warte zehn Minuten auf dich.
pairs.english: I am waiting ten minutes for you.
